newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX crude oil tumbles on Iraq, API weekly.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX crude oil tumbles on Iraq, API weekly.

text.p: NYMEX crude oil futures settled sharply lower Tuesday, pulling refined products lower as well, as the market sold off on United States administration's comments that it would approve a renewal of the Iraqi "oil-for-food" accord.

The market sold off further in after-hours trading following the release of the American Petroleum Institute's weekly status report showing rising crude stocks, even while gasoline output hit a record.
Crude oil for July delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange settled 65 cents lower at $20.33 a barrel.
July unleaded gasoline dropped 1.55 cents to end at 61.44 cents a gallon. July heating oil settled at 54.62 cents, down 1.70 cents.
July crude was down another 25 cents just after 1700 EDT after the API report at $20.08 a barrel.
"They look pretty bearish," said Thomas Blakeslee, a Cargill Investors Services trader, referring to the API data.
"Clearly, operations are up pretty sharply here and we're seeing very high supply figures."
Indeed, the API reported that gasoline output for the week ended May 30 was at a record 8.195 million barrels per day, beating the previous record set in December, 1994.
Analysts expect that, after breaking through some key technical support levels on Monday and Tuesday, the market may now be set for some hefty lossses.

Ken Miller, senior principal and Purvin & Gertz Inc, said his firm has a WTI price target of $19 a barrel by August, which slips to $18.50 by the end of the year. Miller sees an average price of $19 a barrel in 1998.

He points to rising production by non-OPEC producers and the potential for unrest among OPEC member nations over lost market share, especially if crude oil prices move toward the area of $16 to $17 a barrel.
"We definitely believe that the fundamentals are deteriorating," Miller said.

"Inventories are building up at a pretty rapid pace. There is little doubt the pressure is going to get quite a bit stronger through the summer and into next year, depending on how major OPEC producers respond to the lack of market share, particularly Saudi Arabia," Miller said.
"There's not enough room for OPEC to continue to produce at its current levels. Something's going to have to give," he said.
Miller said the market was well supplied for the long term unless demand rises considerably.
"I think the gains we have had here over the last several weeks have been due mostly to temporary things like political factors, refinery problems and those sorts of things.
"There's no real long-term support for the prices we have here. We see prices dropping off several dollars a barrel by late summer, and it could get worse," he said.
